theme: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, the first penitential psalm
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 6. This is the first of the seven traditional penitential psalms. Read it as the prayer of someone who is worn out by suffering and has nowhere else to turn.
settingTheScene: Psalm 6 is a prayer of David, with the note “according to The Sheminith,” probably a musical direction. Nothing in it tells us the exact crisis, and that is useful, because it lets many sufferers pray it. David is physically and emotionally exhausted, and he feels that God’s anger is on him. The psalm moves from desperate pleading to a sudden confidence at the end.
observation: “O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath” (v. 1).
“Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am languishing; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled” (v. 2).
“My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O LORD, how long?” (v. 3).
“Turn, O LORD, deliver my life; save me for the sake of your steadfast love” (v. 4).
“For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?” (v. 5).
“I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping” (v. 6).
“Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping” (v. 8).
“The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer” (v. 9).
interpretation:
This psalm holds nothing back. David is weak, his bones are shaking, and his nights are given over to tears. He asks God not to rebuke him in anger. He does not claim to be innocent. He knows that suffering may be connected to sin, and he asks for mercy rather than strict justice. The ground of his appeal is not his own goodness but God’s “steadfast love,” the covenant word that appears again and again in the Psalms.

The question “How long?” is the cry of the sufferer in many psalms. It is not rebellion. It is an honest question brought to God. Believers in the Bible are allowed to ask it. The Bible does not require us to hide our exhaustion behind pious language.

Verse 5 is an argument. David says that the dead cannot praise God, so why let him die? At this point in the story of Scripture, the hope of resurrection is not yet fully revealed, and David’s view of death is dark. The argument is that God’s glory is served by keeping his servant alive to praise him. Later revelation will show that death is not the end for those in God’s hands.

The turn comes without warning. In verse 8, the tone changes: “Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.” Nothing in David’s circumstances has changed. What changed is that he has prayed, and he is sure he has been heard. He says it three times: God has heard my weeping, my plea, my prayer.

The psalm teaches that tears are a form of prayer, and that God hears them. It also teaches that we may leave our suffering with God and trust him with the outcome, even before we see it.
connection: Jesus said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38), and “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). Jesus took on our weakness. John 12:27 echoes verse 3: “Now is my soul troubled.” Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear.
application:
Bring your exhaustion to God without dressing it up. Tell him how long it has been.

Ask for mercy based on his steadfast love, not on your record.

Thank him that he hears the sound of your weeping.
prayerPrompts: Tell God honestly how weary you are.
Ask him to be gracious to you for the sake of his steadfast love.
Thank Jesus for weeping and praying in the same way.
